current.rappels: 4 double-rope rappels from bolted anchors down the East Face, starting climber’s left of M&M Ledge
current.rappel_count_note: Four rappels off bolts, reached by working climber's left from M&M Ledge, and the description that gives that sequence assumes two ropes - four double-rope rappels essentially to the ground. Parties who first rappel from M&M Ledge's own fixed pin-and-wire anchor, which also trends climber's left, count five. No single-rope option is described for this line. The alternative descent, for parties who continue to the true summit rather than rappelling from the ledge, is the standard Liberty Bell notch route - a downclimb east to a two-bolt station and two rappels of about 25 m into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch - which is fewer rappels but lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the East Face approach and from your pack. Per-station distances are not published; the figures given assume near-full-length double-rope rappels.

rappel_detail.notes: First of four double-rope rappels down the East Face, starting near M&M Ledge.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor, climber's-left of M&M Ledge
hazards: The M&M Ledge anchor is two pieces of old fixed gear, a pin and a wire. A large and reportedly bomber horn sits up and left of it that would make a much better station and nobody has rigged it - carry cord if you want to use it
Because the line trends left rather than dropping straight down, a rope end blown or thrown off line is awkward to recover
rappel_detail.station: The rappels begin at M&M Ledge. From it, work climber's left to reach good bolts - the bolted stations are not directly beneath where the ledge drops you, and finding them is the only route-finding on this descent. If you rappel from the ledge's own anchor instead, that is a fixed piton and a fixed wire, and the rappel from it also trends climber's left.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the East Face line on double ropes.
hazards: Steep sustained face with nothing to stand on between stations - once on the rope you are committed to reaching the next anchor
rappel_detail.station: Second station on the bolted line down the East Face.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the East Face line on double ropes.
hazards: Anything knocked off a station here falls the full height of the wall
rappel_detail.station: Third station on the bolted line.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel, reaching the ground at the base of the East Face.
hazards: Talus and snow at the base of the face for much of the season
rappel_detail.station: Last rappel, essentially reaching the ground at the base of the East Face - the side you approached from, so this is where your pack is.

current.descent_text: Two documented options. (1) From the top of the route near M&M Ledge, work climber's left to good bolts and make four double-rope rappels (2 ropes) essentially to the ground at the base of the East Face — this is the faster option and returns you directly to your pack/the East Face approach. (2) If you continue to the true summit instead, descend via the standard Liberty Bell notch route: downclimb east ~100 ft through trees/loose rock to the 2-bolt station, then make two roughly 25m rappels (the second off a bolted anchor) down into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then hike down the scree/snow gully to the climbers' trail along the base of the west faces — but this leaves you on the opposite (west) side of the mountain from your car at the East Face pullout, requiring a shuttle or road walk back.

current.rappel_count_note: Standard/primary Liberty Crack descent, consistently described: two rappels of roughly 25-30m on bolted anchors down to Beckey Gully/the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then hike down the gully. It is the same descent as for Liberty Crack (Free). The four-rap M&M Ledge/East-Face line is real but belongs to Thin Red Line.

rappel_detail.pull: Under 30m, single 60m rope. Do not link this into one double-length rappel to the notch — that variation has a poor reputation for jammed ropes.
rappel_detail.notes: After topping out, traverse third-class ledges climber's left to a bolted anchor in an alcove; first rappel down toward Beckey Gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor (double-bolt station in an alcove near the topout)
hazards: the last few metres to the anchor cross an exposed sloping ledge
the station is genuinely hard to spot from above and parties have rappelled past the line or had to climb back up to find it; note it before you commit to going down
rappel_detail.station: Reached by traversing climber's left along the third-class ledges at the top of the route, or by downclimbing the last pitch of the Beckey Route. The anchor is shiny bolts with chains set in a corner or shallow alcove on a steep wall overlooking the Liberty Bell-Concord notch — you have to look down over the edge a little to see it, and it is not visible from the ledge above.

rappel_detail.pull: About 25m, single 60m rope reaches the notch.
rappel_detail.notes: Second rappel reaches Beckey Gully / the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch; from there downclimb/hike the gully to the climbers' trail.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor (the second station is also described as a tree — judge what is there)
hazards: this last rappel is the one repeatedly reported for stuck ropes, in more than one case costing a party a re-lead of an adjacent route to recover the strand

you are rappelling over a climbing route and above a busy approach gully, so both your rope and anything you knock loose land on other parties — the notch echoes badly enough that shouted communication is unreliable when it is busy
the notch below is snow early or loose scree later, and the gully leading down from it sheds rock readily
rappel_detail.station: A second set of bolts and chains, described as sitting in an alcove with a tree beside it, dropping directly into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch.

current.descent_text:
The standard way off is the two-rappel Beckey-side descent, shared with Liberty Crack (Free), Freedom Rider and the Beckey Route. From the bolted alcove near the summit shoulder where the last pitch ends, traverse third-class ledges climber's left to the double-bolt station - the final few metres to it are exposed - and make the first rappel, under 30 m, down toward Beckey Gully. Do not link this into one double-length rappel to the notch: that variation has a poor reputation for jammed ropes. A second rappel of roughly the same length reaches Beckey Gully and the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch, and from there you downclimb and hike the scree and boulder gully below the notch - snow-covered or loose and unpleasant depending on the season - to the climbers' trail and the Blue Lake Trail. Manage the ropes carefully on both: the terrain is steep and snags are the common problem here.

Plan the walk back before you start down. Liberty Crack parties park at the East Face pullout on SR-20 rather than at the Blue Lake Trailhead, so this descent puts you down on the far side of the mountain from the car, meaning either a shuttle or roughly a mile back along the highway shoulder. A rappel line down the east face that returns you directly to your packs at the base of the route has been reported - a bolted line of six stations on the right side of the wall, where a single 60 m rope reaches each station but is tight at a couple of them, so parties carry a second rope or plan a short downclimb. The four-rappel line off M&M Ledge is a real descent, but it belongs to Thin Red Line rather than to this route; do not plan on it here.

current.rappels: 3 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope on the standard Liberty Bell descent: one off slung trees just below the summit, then two of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. Downclimbing the first section instead leaves two.
current.rappel_count_note: This route finishes on Liberty Bell and takes the standard descent. Three rappels on a single 60 m rope, which is the rope this route recommends and the configuration these three stations describe. The count of two comes from the same station set rather than a different one: the first rappel, off the trees, is optional and replaces a downclimb of the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem, so a party that downclimbs that section starts at the second station and reaches the ground in two single-rope rappels. Accounts recording two and accounts recording three are describing the same anchors. The two lower rappels are reported at about 25 m each, and a single 60 m rope reaches the first ledge with room to spare. This is the standard descent line shared with the East Face and Northwest Face routes. Parties who stop at M&M Ledge can instead descend Thin Red Line’s two-rope line: one rappel off the ledge and four more off bolts down the East Face.

rappel_detail.pull: A single 60 m rope reaches the ledge with room to spare. Knot both ends as a matter of habit.
rappel_detail.notes: Reached by downclimbing the upper pitch about 20 ft from the summit, then moving left (east). First of the three single-rope rappels.
hazards: These trees are the only marker for the top of the descent and are easy to walk past on the summit ridge; a party that misses them commits itself to downclimbing the loose east gully instead.
The lower tree's slings are periodically found tired. Carry cord or webbing to replace rather than rappelling on whatever happens to be there.
Snow can linger on the landing ledge into early season.
rappel_detail.station: Reverse the last pitch roughly 15-20 m (about 50 ft) from the summit and work toward the Concord Tower side of the crest. The anchor is a tree carrying fixed slings, tucked off the crest near a shallow groove in the rock; two slung trees stand close together and the upper one is the sounder of the pair. It is much easier to pick out while leading pitch 4 than from above, so note it on the way up. The rappel lands on a sandy, tree-dotted ledge.

rappel_detail.pull: A plumb pull off bolts. Keep the strands clear of the ledge lip and its trees so nothing catches on the retrieve.
rappel_detail.notes: Second station, on a large ledge reached by scrambling down and to the right from the first rappel.
hazards: Loose sand and grit on the ledge above slabby downclimbing.
If the chains are not found after the ropes are pulled, the party is stranded between stations with no anchor.
rappel_detail.station: Do not rappel straight on from the sandy ledge. Work right along the ledge, then down, then right again to reach a fixed station of bolts and chains on the steep wall. Parties consistently report this hardware as hard to spot, so scout it before pulling the first rope.

rappel_detail.pull: Because the rappel is diagonal, the pull strand drags across the wall and this descent has a documented history of jammed ropes. One party had to fix one strand, lead back up the climbable ground to free it, then ascend to the station and re-rig. Feed the pull strand out and away from the diagonal, and pull from the notch rather than from directly under the anchor.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappels somewhat diagonally into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Downclimb the gully from there to the packs.
hazards: The line traverses, so anyone who loses the stance swings across the wall.
The notch and the gully below it are loose, and anything dislodged here funnels onto the climbers' path that other parties are walking up.
rappel_detail.station: The lowest fixed station on the wall, straight below the previous one. The rappel from it runs slightly diagonally rather than plumb and finishes in the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at roughly 7,300 ft, close to where most parties leave packs at the top of the approach gully.

current.descent_text: Live Free or Die climbs the East Face for 8 pitches to M&M Ledge (roughly mid-height), then shares its final 3-4 pitches to the summit with the upper section of Thin Red Line. Parties who finish on the summit take the standard Liberty Bell descent. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail. Parties who stop at M&M Ledge can instead take Thin Red Line’s rappel line: from M&M Ledge, rappel with two ropes off a fixed pin and wire, then work climber’s left to bolted anchors and make four more double-rope rappels to the talus at the base of the East Face.

current.descent_text: Most parties reverse the ascent line, downclimbing and rappelling the same southwest gully/couloir system (the X Couloir) back down into the southwest basin below the face. This is a real rappelling descent, not a walk-off: the most detailed documented descent (a repeat/'2nd descent' trip report) describes 10 double-rope rappels — 4 off pickets placed by the descending party, 1 off a sling around a rock, and 5 off pre-existing slings left around rock horns lower in the gully. Bring a rope long enough to rappel on doubled strands plus spare cord/webbing for building or backing up anchors, since fixed tat should never be trusted blindly. Anchors are a mix of natural (slung rock horns and blocks) and improvised (snow pickets), not bolted — expect to build some yourself. The exact rappel count is conditions-dependent: earlier-season parties with more continuous snow have gotten down with as few as 3 rappels off deadman/picket anchors and simul-downclimbing between them, while later-season, rockier conditions push the count up toward the 10-rappel figure above; budget for the higher number and extra anchor material. The gully funnels rockfall and is exposed to spindrift/small slides after storms, so descend early and move efficiently through the narrower constrictions. Once off the couloir, re-rope for the bergschrund and any crevassed ground on the way down to the treeline camp, then reverse the approach - down past East Rankin Lake and around Pt. 4481 on the old decommissioned road - back to FR-38. Do not descend north toward Heliotrope Ridge. With a camp in the Rankin Creek basin, going that way puts you on the opposite side of the mountain with a glacier between you and your camp.

current.rappels: Two rappels on the descent. One party made a double-60 m rappel from near the top of the line and a second rappel down from the col southeast of the summit; they noted a single 60 m rope would have been enough for the col rappel. Anchors are not fixed — bring cord and tat, and expect to build off rock horns or leave a picket/screw.
current.rappel_count_note: Two rappels, from one winter party's account: a double-rope rappel near the top of the line, and a single-rope rappel from the col southeast of the summit. Bring cord and tat; nothing is fixed.

current.rappel_count_note: Four rappels on two 60 m ropes: every rappel needs both ropes. Nearly every anchor is bolted below the top trees, and some rappels are diagonal, so steer to stay on line. About an hour from the top to the base. Instead of rappelling, you can traverse off to a 3rd-class ramp partway down.

current.descent_text: Descend via rappel using two ropes; expect some diagonal-rappel maneuvering to stay on anchors, or traverse off to a 3rd-class ramp partway down. Figure roughly an hour from the summit/top of the route back to the base.
